title: Buffett on reporting to owners
lede: Buffett writes to his owners as he would want a manager to write to him. The partnership letters set the habit of stating his thinking and his doubts plainly. The Berkshire letters turn it into rules: the CEO writes the report himself, the numbers shown are the ones he uses, bad news is told plainly, no guidance is given, and every owner hears it at the same time.

entries.excerpt: the partners are certainly entitled to know what I am thinking in this regard even though the nature of the business is such as to introduce a high probability of error in such expectations.
entries.note: Early on he shares his expectations with partners and says plainly how likely they are to be wrong.

entries.excerpt: behavior most distasteful which publicly announces one set of goals and motivations when actually an entirely different set of factors prevails.
entries.note: Lowering his own targets, he ties candour to stated goals that match the real ones.

entries.excerpt: Your Chairman has a firm belief that owners are entitled to hear directly from the CEO as to what is going on and how he evaluates the business, currently and prospectively.
entries.note: The annual report becomes the CEO's own job, not one for a staff specialist or PR adviser.

entries.excerpt: Our guideline is to tell you the business facts that we would want to know if our positions were reversed.  We owe you no less.
entries.note: The owner principles set the test he keeps for decades: report what you would want in their place.

entries.excerpt: The only business matters that are off limits at the annual meeting are those about which candor might cost our company real money.  Our activities in securities would be the main example.
entries.note: The annual meeting takes every question, with one narrow exception that protects the owners themselves.

entries.excerpt: You can be sure that we will immediately report to you in detail if the underlying economics or competitive position of any of these businesses should materially change.
entries.note: Brief write-ups of stable businesses come with a promise to speak up at once when things change.

entries.excerpt: At Berkshire, we believe in Charlie's dictum - "Just tell me the bad news; the good news will take care of itself" - and that is the behavior we expect of our managers when they are reporting to us.
entries.note: He holds himself to the rule he sets for managers and reports on three slipping businesses.

entries.excerpt: But if it is “earnings guidance” or the like that shareholders or analysts seek, we will simply guide them to our public documents.
entries.note: With thousands of new holders after General Re, he restates that no earnings guidance will be offered.

entries.excerpt: Charlie and I think it is both deceptive and dangerous for CEOs to predict growth rates for their companies. They are, of course, frequently egged on to do so by both analysts and their own investor relations departments.
entries.note: Public growth targets are now named as a cause of operating and accounting games.

entries.excerpt: We are suspicious of those CEOs who regularly claim they do know the future – and we become downright incredulous if they consistently reach their declared targets. Managers that always promise to “make the numbers” will at some point be tempted to make up the numbers.
entries.note: After Enron, a steady record of hitting forecasts reads as a warning sign in its own right.

entries.excerpt: When we report to you, we will continue to separate out these figures (as we do realized investment gains and losses) so that you can more clearly view the earnings of our operating businesses.
entries.note: Derivative swings are shown apart, so owners see the operating earnings he watches himself.

entries.excerpt: We do not talk one-on-one to large institutional investors or analysts, but rather treat all shareholders the same.
entries.note: Fair reporting covers timing too: every owner gets the news at once, with no private briefings.

entries.excerpt: Our position carries with it the responsibility to report to you what we would like to know if we were the absentee owner and you were the manager.
entries.note: Nearly forty years on, the 1983 test returns almost word for word.

entries.excerpt: Furthermore, Bertie, and her three daughters as well, have a large portion of their savings in Berkshire shares. Their ownership spans decades, and every year Bertie will read what I have to say. My job is to anticipate her questions and give her honest answers.
entries.note: The imagined reader gets a name: his sister, a long-term holder owed honest answers.

entries.excerpt: This approach leads us to an annual recitation of both good and bad developments at the many businesses you indirectly own through your Berkshire shares.
entries.note: His last letter as CEO frames the report as a duty beyond the mandated figures.
